title: Shuka's clear sight
hookLine: bathing women stay as they are when a young sage walks by, and cover up for his well-known father
carry: the self is pure; practice clears the mind
tomorrow: an asura wins a deadly boon
last: TIME IS A WHEEL OF AGES, LIVED ONE INSTANT AT A TIME.

lines: VYASA WALKS PAST. THEY COVER UP.
cards: Shuka, son of the great sage Vyasa, is young, and he's leaving home for good, wandering with nothing, not even clothes. His father follows, calling after him.

On the way they pass a pool where celestial women, apsaras, are bathing. Shuka walks right past, and the women don't move. A moment later old Vyasa comes by, fully dressed, and they hurry to cover themselves.
Vyasa stops, puzzled. Why for me, and not for him?

teach.b: The Bhagavata gives their answer in one line. You still see man and woman. Your son's sight is pure.
Shuka wasn't stronger than his father; Vyasa is among the greatest sages there are. Shuka's mind simply added nothing of its own to what he saw, and everyone at that pool could feel the difference.
The self, the atman, is already pure. It was never stained, and Vedanta teachers often call it ever-pure. What gets cloudy is the mind.
So Hindus speak of chitta-shuddhi, purifying the mind, and say that's what puja, fasting, chanting and service are for. They don't wash the self. They wipe the glass.
Patanjali ends his third book right there.

teach.h: 3.55: WHEN THE TWO PURITIES ARE EQUAL.
teach.b: Sutra 3.55: when the purity of the mind's clearest part, sattva, equals the purity of the seer, kaivalya. Freedom. Kaivalya comes from kevala: alone, whole, standing on its own.
And the classical commentary adds a line that clears the table after weeks of strange powers: this freedom comes whether or not someone has the powers.
Invisibility, strength, knowing other minds, the gods at the door: none of it was required.

teach.h: THE SELF IS PURE; PRACTICE CLEARS THE MIND.
teach.b: A mind like clean glass is. Shuka didn't fly or vanish at that pool. He just saw, without adding anything, and that was the whole difference.

how: Hindus often describe puja, fasting, chanting and service as chitta-shuddhi, purifying the mind, while the self (atman) is held to be already pure; many begin worship with water as a sign of purification, and teachers stress that kaivalya does not depend on any powers.

o: freedom: the seer standing alone, whole, untangled
the greatest power, earned at the end of book three
a lonely life, cut off from other people

games.q: the clean glass — tap the pairs.

s: in the story, the apsaras covered up for Shuka
they covered for old Vyasa, not for Shuka; his sight was pure.
Hindus say puja cleans the self
the self is already pure; practice purifies the mind.
the commentary says kaivalya comes with or without the powers
what matters is the mind's purity equaling the seer's.

games.q: a friend asks: if Hindus say the self is already perfect, why bother with daily puja?
o: no reason; puja is just habit.
puja polishes the self until it becomes perfect.
the self's already pure; puja clears the mind so it can show.
games.why: Hindus call it chitta-shuddhi, purifying the mind. the atman needs no cleaning, so all the work is on the glass, as in sutra 3.55.

practice: Many families begin puja by sprinkling a few drops of water and remembering God as the one who makes things pure. If you pray, begin that way. If you don't, rinse your hands slowly.

Then rest on the breath and notice what the mind is adding right now: a mood, a judgment, a story about how this is going. Don't scrub. Let it settle, like silt in a glass of water, and look through again.

wordCard.voice: Kaivalya: freedom, from kevala, alone and whole. When the mind is as clear as the seer, the seer stands free, with or without any powers.

orig.note: Sanskrit citta-śuddhi: purity of mind (citta, mind; śuddhi, cleanness), what many Hindus say practice is for.

carryVoice: Your line: the self is pure; practice clears the mind. Book three of the Yoga Sutras, done.
